reason: The sources support 16 atomic claims, each verified by at least two distinct websites.
story: In 1997, Russia's Mir space station suffered two major disasters within four months. In February, an oxygen canister ignited in the Kvant-1 module, filling the station with smoke for 14 minutes while the crew fought it with fire extinguishers. Then on June 25, during a manual docking experiment, commander Vasily Tsibliyev lost control of the uncrewed Progress M-34 cargo ship. The seven-ton vessel slammed into the Spektr module, damaging a solar panel and puncturing Mir's hull. As air hissed into space and pressure dropped, the crew frantically severed power and air cables running through the open hatch and sealed off Spektr. Isolating the module deprived Mir of half its electrical power, causing the station to tumble out of control. The crew used thrusters on their docked Soyuz craft to arrest the spin and stabilize Mir, narrowly saving the space station.
angle: To save Mir from depressurizing after a cargo ship collision, cosmonauts had to cut live electrical cables by hand and permanently seal off a whole module.

claims.claim: In February 1997, a backup solid-fuel oxygen canister caught fire inside Russia's Mir space station.
The oxygen canister fire burned for 14 minutes inside the space station.
Heavy smoke filled Mir during the fire, forcing crew members to wear breathing respirators.
The uncrewed Progress M-34 cargo spacecraft launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome on April 6, 1997.
Progress M-34 docked with Mir on April 8, 1997, delivering food, water, oxygen, and repair supplies.
Progress M-34 undocked from Mir on June 24, 1997, to prepare for a manual docking test.
On June 25, 1997, Progress M-34 collided with Mir during a manual remote-controlled docking attempt.
Cosmonaut Vasily Tsibliyev was manually remote-piloting the Progress M-34 cargo craft when it struck the station.
The collision punctured the hull of Mir's Spektr science module, starting an air leak into space.
The impact damaged a solar array attached to the Spektr module.
The crew sealed off the depressurized Spektr module by disconnecting and cutting cables across the hatchway.
Isolating Spektr deprived Mir of roughly half of its electrical power supply.
Following the collision, Mir lost main attitude control and began tumbling in orbit.
The crew stabilized Mir's spin using thrusters on the docked Soyuz spacecraft.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev suffered a heart arrhythmia during the stressful aftermath of the collision.
Progress M-34 was deorbited and destroyed over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1997.

disputed: The primary cause of the Progress M-34 trajectory error is cited as a cargo mass miscalculation in one account (S1) versus visual distance judgment limitations without radar guidance in others (S4, S5); a script should focus on the lack of radar guidance during the test approach.

The cause of Commander Tsibliyev's medical condition is attributed to heart arrhythmia from stress in some sources (S1, S5) and abnormal sleep schedules in another (S3); attribute specific medical causes if mentioned.
